transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-25
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (scheduled)
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Mei Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Aurora Head of AI), Priya Singh (Infra), Sam O'Connor (Platform)

Summary: Quick walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations focusing on batching and prefix/KV caching to reduce per-token cost for Aurora's document summarization pipeline. Covered tradeoffs for latency, cache hit rates, model variants, and suggested pilot to measure savings with Aurora's traffic profile.

Topics: batching strategies, KV/prefix cache tuning, cost model walk-through, quantization impacts, dedicated vs hosted routing, telemetry/metrics to collect for pilot

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh welcome. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood team. We also have Mei, our systems SE who will do most of the deep dive. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Alex: Good, thanks. Excited to see how we can slice down our inference bill. We've got a pretty heavy summarization workload, multiple long documents, average output lengths vary.
[00:18] Priya: Hi, yeah from infra perspective we care about latency tail and predictable peaks. We have daily batch jobs and also interactive summarization for our analyst UI.
[00:27] Mei: Great context, thanks. Quick agenda: we'll run through high-level Optimize recommendations (batching, prefix/KV cache), show cost-model examples, and then propose a pilot footprint to measure real savings. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:39] Sam: Sounds good.
[00:41] Mei: Alright, first, batching. So there are two axes: horizontal batching (multiple independent requests batched onto the same GPU in the runtime) and request-level batching (token-level packing). For Aurora, because you have a mix of short interactive requests and longer summarizations, we usually recommend a dual-policy: small low-latency route for interactive and a cost-optimized route that aggressively batches background summarization.
[01:05] Alex: Can you give ballpark numbers? Like if we go from no batching to a 4-6x effective batch, what does that look like cost-wise?
[01:12] Mei: Sure, in our model examples, when throughput is the bottleneck, moving from batch size 1 to effective 4 can reduce per-token GPU time by ~2.5-3x depending on padding inefficiencies and kernel selection. That maps to roughly 40-60% token cost reduction before you consider cache wins.
[01:32] Jordan: Important caveat: latency-sensitive UI traffic should be routed to the low-latency lane. We can configure autoscaling and burst capacity so the UI stays snappy.
[01:42] Priya: How do you handle mixed workloads? We worry about batch tail affecting user p95.
[01:47] Mei: Two things: routing policies at the API layer — route by route or by token budget — and preemption with reserved capacity. Plus our continuous batching uses time windows so interactive short requests can be served immediately with minimal queuing.
[01:59] Jordan: Also note you can set per-route SLOs and Redwood will try to respect them with autoscale/priority policies.
[02:07] Alex: Okay good. Next, prefix and KV cache.
[02:10] Mei: Right. For your summarization pipeline, most of the work is reusing the same document context or similar prefixes across requests. A prefix cache stores the decoded KV cache for commonly seen prefixes so subsequent calls skip recomputing the early layers. In our cost models, a 30-50% cache hit rate on long documents can cut token compute by up to 40% because the first N tokens are effectively free on cache hit.
[02:36] Sam: Do you cache across users? We have PII concerns, so we need to scope cache by tenancy and possibly encrypt.
[02:43] Mei: Yes, caches are tenancy-scoped and for Private deployments we integrate with your KMS for keying. For Hosted we support per-tenant isolation and optional TTL enforcement. We'll send the security doc but short answer, you can bound cache keys by user or doc id and control TTL.
[02:58] Priya: What's the memory cost for a big doc KV cache? For a 20k token doc, how big are caches and what are the eviction strategies?
[03:06] Mei: Good question. A 20k token KV cache on a T5-like architecture is several GBs per shard; we shard the cache across GPUs and we provide LRU-based eviction plus pinning for hot documents. For enterprise/dedicated pools, we can provision extra GPU memory or use a hybrid TTL + size policy. We'll capture your expected doc sizes in the pilot spec.
[03:25] Alex: You mentioned prefix vs full KV cache, can you clarify?
[03:29] Mei: Prefix cache stores the initial prefix KVs — think system prompts, document headings, or previous conversation history — whereas full KV caching would store the whole doc encoding. Prefix is cheaper and hits more often when many requests share the same initial context. Full KV is useful for session-resume or long single-document pipelines.
[03:45] Jordan: One practical tip — for summarization we often combine prefix caching for templates + chunk-level KV for very large docs and stitch outputs. That keeps memory bounded.
[03:55] Alex: Nice. Walk me through the cost model for both.
[03:58] Mei: Sure. We model cost as compute_time * GPU_cost + infra amortized + storage for caches. In the spreadsheet I'll send, we show scenarios: baseline (no batching/no cache), batching only, cache only, and batching+cache combined. Typical savings we see: batching cuts 30-60% and cache adds another 20-40% depending on hit rate. Combined you can often see 60-80% reduction for batch-friendly workloads.
[04:28] Sam: How accurate are these numbers for our real traffic?
[04:31] Mei: They depend on token distribution. That's why the pilot is important — we replay your token histogram against the runtime. If you share 30 days of anonymized token histograms and sample prompts, we can run a bench and produce a tailored cost forecast.
[04:45] Priya: We can provide that. Slight question on quantization — do you recommend 4-bit quant or int8 for us? We care about latency and slight quality differences matter.
[04:55] Mei: If you need max throughput and can tolerate tiny quality deltas, 4-bit dynamic quantization with Redwood-verified profiles often gives 1.2-1.8x throughput improvement over fp16 on some open models. For careful quality-sensitive diffs, we recommend running evals on your prompt set; our Optimize recommendations include model+quantization pairings. We'll include suggested quant profiles in the spreadsheet.
[05:17] Alex: Good. On security/compliance — SOC2, audit logs, SSO — can we get the docs?
[05:22] Jordan: Yes, I'll attach SOC 2 docs, SAML SSO integration guide, and the security appendix for Private deployments.
[05:28] Priya: Also need network egress controls and VPC peering notes.
[05:32] Jordan: Yep, we'll include the VPC checklist.
[05:35] Mei: Back to telemetry — to measure pilot success we recommend collecting: per-route p50/p95 latency, batch sizes, cache hit rate (prefix vs full), token-in/token-out distribution, and GPU cumulative compute seconds. We'll provide a Prometheus + Grafana dashboard template.
[05:50] Sam: Can your runtime export those metrics to our prometheus stack?
[05:53] Mei: Yes, both hosted and private options can push metrics; for hosted we can set up a read-only metrics endpoint or forward metrics to your workspace.
[06:02] Alex: Ok, next steps recap?
[06:05] Jordan: Action items: Jordan will send the cost-model workbook, security docs, and a sample pilot plan by next week. Priya will send token histograms and sample prompts. Mei will stand up a benchmark harness and run baseline vs batching+cache tests once we have the data. We aim for initial pilot numbers within two weeks after data receipt.
[06:24] Priya: Sounds good. One more quick Q: do you have an internal SLA for cache consistency? We worried about staleness if docs update.
[06:31] Mei: TTLs and invalidation hooks are supported; you can call a cache-invalidate API on document update. For strong consistency cases we recommend bypassing cache for write/read immediately after update.
[06:41] Alex: Great, appreciate the demo.
[06:43] Jordan: Thanks all. We'll follow up with materials. Meeting end.
